Chapter 9: Managing Complexity and Scaling Improvement
As organizations grow, things start to get a little more complicated, don’t they? You’ve got more products, more locations, maybe even new customer segments—suddenly, managing all the moving parts and spotting bottlenecks isn’t as straightforward as it used to be.
But here’s the good news. The core principles for improvement? They don’t change. What does change is how you apply them. You’ll need more coordination, and definitely more clarity.
One approach that works well is breaking big systems into smaller, manageable chunks. Think of it like this: if you’re running a global company, you might treat each plant or each region as its own little system. Each one gets its own clear goal and way to measure progress. That way, you can use the Five Focusing Steps locally, while still keeping everyone aligned with the bigger company mission.
Now, as things scale up, communication becomes absolutely essential. What happens if one team makes a big improvement, but it causes trouble for another? Regular cross-functional meetings are a lifesaver here—they help make sure everyone’s pulling in the same direction. And when everyone can see shared dashboards or visual management tools, it’s much easier to stay on top of priorities and track progress together.
Here’s something else to keep in mind: constraints don’t just show up on the factory floor. They can exist at all sorts of levels. Maybe it’s an operational constraint, like a slow machine. Or maybe it’s something bigger—like limited demand in the market, or even regulatory roadblocks. The trick for leaders is learning to “zoom in and out”—solving the day-to-day bottlenecks, but never losing sight of the bigger picture.
There are a few practical tools that can make this easier:
First: process mapping. This lets you actually see how work moves across departments or locations, so you can spot where things get stuck.
Next: constraint heat maps. These help you pinpoint where bottlenecks are most likely to pop up.
And finally: scenario planning. This is about thinking ahead—asking, “If we make a change here, how will it ripple out to the rest of the system?”
When you approach complexity with a mix of curiosity and structure, you open the door to ongoing improvement—even as your organization grows and changes.
So, no matter how complex things get, you’ll always have a way forward.
